node.name: Demystifying the Literature Review
node.descriptionText: Learn how to conduct a literature review for your research papers, independent projects, and fellowship applications.
node.descriptionHtml:
Learn how to conduct a literature review for your research papers, independent projects, and fellowship applications. 

Attendees will learn:  

  • Why a literature review is important and how it can help your research  
  • Strategies to find relevant literature  
  • Techniques to synthesize the literature  
  •  How citation management software (like Zotero) can help facilitate a literature review  

 

What is a literature review?  

A literature review is a narrative and synthesis about a set of sources. They are often required in theses and published papers to provide an analysis of sources/authors to demonstrate how your research fits within a larger academic conversation.  While not the same as a systematic review, scoping review, comprehensive review, or meta-analysis, those research methodologies draw from essential literature review skills, so this workshop is still a great place to start.  

Audience: Undergraduate students in all disciplines. Graduate students new to writing a literature review are also welcome to attend.  

Workshop Incentive Program: Any student who attends at least 3 library workshops this semester will be eligible to receive a FREE Yale Library tote bag. Learn more.

node.name: Daily Worship and Communion at Marquand Chapel
node.descriptionText:
Join us at 11:30am in Marquand Chapel for our daily worship.

Worship in Marquand often draws on a wide variety of inherited Christian traditions, with the worship of many denominations being represented. Beyond that, though, we also pay attention to the rising number of people in Western society who have a lively interest in spirituality but feel no connection to traditional forms of church and worship. So Marquand is also actively engaged in original, creative, and experimental forms of worship, both for committed Christians and for those exploring the faith.

node.name: Learning That Vulnerability is Strength with Eugene Z. Bertrand, LMSW
node.descriptionText: Join us for an engaging conversation with Eugene Z. Bertrand, LMSW, moderated by Earl McCoy Jr., exploring what it means to embrace vulnerability as a source of strength rather than weakness. Together, we’ll unpack the pressures that often keep us from being open, asking for support, and showing up authentically. Through reflection and meaningful dialogue, participants will discover how vulnerability can deepen connection, strengthen leadership, and support personal growth. Come ready to challenge old perceptions and redefine what strength can look like.

node.name: Ross Martin's Qualifying Exam
node.descriptionText:
Ross Martin will stand for the Qualifying Examination for acceptance into candidacy for the Ph.D. degree on Friday, November 13 at 2:00 PM via Zoom. All faculty (only faculty) are welcome and invited to attend. Copies of Ross’ dissertation prospectus and qualifying exam questions and answers and Zoom link can be obtained from the Doctoral Program Office (contact: elisabeth.barsa@yale.edu). 
Committee members: 
•	Prof. Justin Farrell (Chair)
•	Prof. Os Schmitz
•	Prof. Chris Cannon (Univ. Alaska-Fairbanks)

Instructions: Answer every question below. Demonstrate the breadth and depth of your knowledge developed in your elective courses and directed reading. 

YSE Note on AI: YSE uses Pangram, an artificial intelligence (AI) writing detection tool, to help maintain high academic integrity standards. Submitted assignments may be reviewed by Pangram via YSE’s Academic Affairs team as part of a holistic academic integrity review. For additional information on YSE’s academic integrity policies and its use of Pangram, please see YSE’s Personal and Academic Standards, and Disciplinary Procedures.

Section I: TEK Theory

It is well established in the literature that traditional ecological knowledge (TEK) is valuable. We know that wildlife and conservation science and associated bureaucratic institutions have historically marginalized it. However, efforts to better incorporate it raise thorny questions about legitimacy and power. 

Drawing on major traditions within this interdisciplinary field, assess the current state of TEK research and how modern science is including it in their analyses. What are the most important theoretical debates about its inclusion, especially the degree to which the inclusion of TEK in modern wildlife and conservation science aligns with the full scope of TEK? What important questions remain unanswered? What could constitute a genuinely new contribution to the integration of TEK with wildlife and conservation science? 

Section II: Gwich’in Socialization and Epistemology 

Drawing on primary and secondary Gwich’in sources, explain how Gwich’in culture forms their epistemology. Using specific examples from Gwich’in cosmology, spirituality, language, customary laws, or oral stories, explain how these cultural elements form a knowledge system that is learned and passed between generations. What are the actual mechanisms of socialization, and what evidence supports your claim?

Finally, how do these processes vary across people within Gwich’in life? Who gets to define what counts as authentic Gwich’in knowledge, and how is that authority established and maintained?

Section III: Direct Experience and the Production of Knowledge

Wildlife and conservation science has used various approaches and technologies to study and gain knowledge about ecology, demography, movements and spatial occurrence of wildlife species. As well, hunters, ranchers, fishers, and others develop practical knowledge through years of direct experience with particular environments.

Drawing on theory from sociology, psychology, and related fields, examine the generalized relationship between direct experience and knowledge. 

Briefly review the various approaches that have been used to understand the life-history and ecology of wildlife species and the degree to which each gives firsthand practical scientific knowledge.

Explain whether direct experience of hunters, ranchers, and fishers reveals firsthand knowledge that wildlife and conservation scientists and their methods do not or cannot? Under what conditions do these approaches converge or diverge? 

Relatedly, consider whether direct experience within TEK is similar or different to other forms of settler practical knowledge developed over generations of close experience with particular environments. What, if anything, makes TEK direct experience distinctive? Are these differences matters of degree or of kind?

Section IV: Empirical Research Methods

Part I: Gwich’in Ethnographic Analysis 

Drawing on your existing ethnographic research, select a substantial passage from your field notes or interviews. Apply a rigorous qualitative method to identify patterns and develop explanations concerning Gwich’in and wildlife. Explain how you move from particular observations to general conclusions, and how you would test those conclusions against other evidence. What contradictory evidence might challenge your interpretations? 

Part II: Wildlife policy analysis

Select a substantive wildlife management document produced by the state of Alaska or federal agencies working in Alaska. Analyze how these institutions produce and justify ecological knowledge. Compare your findings with Part I. Where is there divergence, and what explains these differences? If these diverge, how much are these differences driven by fundamentally different epistemologies versus some other factor(s)?

Part III: Your Role as Social Scientist

Consider your own position as a researcher. Is your approach closer to TEK, Western science, or something else? How do you produce knowledge through ethnography, and what makes your findings credible to (1) Gwich’in people, (2) the scientific community, (3) wildlife management agencies? Evaluate your research against different standards of validity in social science. What claims can your research support, what claims it cannot support, and why?

node.name: Behind the Art: A Guided Tour of the Yale University Art Gallery
node.descriptionText:
Ever wondered what treasures are hiding inside Yale’s art galleries and museums? Join us for a guided visit to the Yale University Art Gallery, one of the oldest university galleries in the United States!
With collections spanning thousands of years and cultures from around the world, the gallery is home to everything from ancient artifacts to modern and contemporary art. Whether you’re an art enthusiast or simply curious to explore somewhere new, this is a great opportunity to discover some of Yale’s incredible collections and learn a little more about the art and history behind them.

node.name: AI for Research and Writing Series Part 2
node.descriptionText:
Using artificial intelligence for research and writing has emerged as a helpful skillset in any scholar’s toolkit. AI tools can find sources, read and summarize articles, write text and code, manage workflows, and identify impactful research questions. In this workshop series, participants will reflect on their own research to identify opportunities for AI to boost their productivity and impact. Through hands-on practice with AI tools adopted by Yale, participants will explore how AI can advance their projects at each stage of the writing process. Join us for:

Intro to AI for Literature Reviews and Reading (11/6)
Intro to AI for Writing (11/13)
Workflow Management with AI (11/20)

Intended audience: Graduate students in all disciplines.
